author: jmilkbal
cardQuote: I feel like I'm beating a dead horse, but I really can not grasp what the catalysts are for creating Rust or Go or Julia or other new languages that want to be safe, reliable, readable, etc..
quote:
I feel like I'm beating a dead horse, but I really can not grasp what the catalysts are for creating Rust or Go or Julia or other new languages that want to be safe, reliable, readable, etc..  30 years ago these problems were solved in a language Ada.  Its exact requirements include all of those and more.

See for yourselves: http://www.adahome.com/History/Steelman/steelman.htm
Later revisions have well-though-out rationales that show off all the changes:
Ada 95: http://www.adaic.org/resources/add_content/standards/95rat/r...
Ada 2005: http://www.adaic.org/ada-resources/standards/ada05/
Ada 2012(!!): http://www2.adacore.com/wp-content/uploads/2006/03/Ada2012_R...

The steelman was the end revision of requirements for the original language.  There is a comparison of C/C++/Java/Ada wrt the steelman available as well.  Ada has become so much more since this document and it's original version one really must see it to be believe it. :o)

As a community we have a tendency to embark on projects on a whim, but the effort, time and money required to bring a language to maturity is enormous.  Even then any deficiency a preexisting language may have surely is not so insurmountable as to make it viable to develop a new language in house.

Can we please have some sanity?  Can we please look for mature solutions?

Edit: Ada has an amazing GCC frontend developed largely by a successful opensource company (with just massive customers across the globe) and is available across all of its targets: the bsd's, solaris, linux, mac, haiku, android and more.  It's a great solution that is hard to ignore.
outcome: Rust 1.0 shipped in 2015; the Linux kernel merged Rust support in 2022.
outcomeDetail: Mozilla's Rust hit 1.0 three years after this comment and became a standard choice for systems code. Firefox, AWS, Microsoft and the Linux kernel adopted it, and Rust repeatedly topped Stack Overflow's most-loved language poll.
note: jmilkbal argued Ada had already solved safety and reliability, making Rust redundant. Rust's ownership model, Cargo and industrial adoption proved different enough to matter.

author: jrockway
cardQuote: I am not sure why I'd use this language with no libraries when I could use a better-designed language with no libraries instead.
quote:
Yeah.  Languages with no control flow other than "call" and "return" were ok for the 80s... but we know better now.  Just add continuations and you get functions, coroutines, exceptions, loop exits ("last", "next", etc.), and so on for free.

I am not sure why I'd use this language with no libraries when I could use a better-designed language with no libraries instead.
outcome: Docker and Kubernetes are written in Go; Go 1.0 shipped in 2012.
outcomeDetail: Go launched in November 2009 and reached 1.0 in March 2012. Its standard library, fast builds and goroutines made it the language of cloud infrastructure; Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform and Prometheus are all written in Go.
note: jrockway's 'no libraries' line ignored Go's substantial standard library, and the ecosystem grew into one of the largest in backend engineering.

author: rljy
cardQuote: I don't see a convincing case for a new language here. This kind of incrementalism is not worth another persons years of effort to create a parallel path.
quote:
I think that it is sad that we keep on creating new programming languages that are not radically different. The Zig language ecosystem faces the same problems as C and the compiler will preform many of the same tasks, lexing, parsing, optimizing, documentation, supporting all sorts of weird edge cases and use cases. From what I see in the introduction, I don't see a convincing case for a new language here. This kind of incrementalism is not worth another persons years of effort to create a parallel path.

I think that if you are going to spend years creating a new language, you ought at least to try something new. Otherwise, you become just another amateur landscape artists. Maybe you're paintings will look nice, but they'll never really be of any great value to society.
storyTitle: Zig Programming Language 0.1.1: First beta release
outcome: Bun, TigerBeetle and Ghostty are written in Zig; Zig 0.14 shipped in 2025.
outcomeDetail: Zig's first beta landed in 2017 and the language attracted serious infrastructure projects. Bun's JavaScript runtime, TigerBeetle's database and Ghostty's terminal are all written in Zig, and the Zig Software Foundation funds full-time work.
note: Zig is still pre-1.0, so the maturity concern was fair. The claim that it had no value to society was not: it became a credible C replacement with real production users.

author: metajack
cardQuote: My team and I evaluated using Elixir for game scripting on an Erlang-based engine, but ended up passing because if we were going to teach the scripters Erlang semantics, we might as well just use Erlang.
quote:
Having rebinding of the vars and dictionary literals are really nice. The syntax feels a bit awkward in general. Commas have to be in non-obvious places, and the "do" keyword is essentially hard-coded. But these aren't huge problems. The homoiconicity looks quite interesting.

The bigger problem is that it still has 90% of Erlang's semantics, and that turns out to be just as different in Ruby-like syntax as it is in Prolog-like syntax. I should note that this isn't a problem for me, but if the aim is to make the language more familiar to others, the syntax change is not much help.

My team and I evaluated using Elixir for game scripting on an Erlang-based engine, but ended up passing because if we were going to teach the scripters Erlang semantics, we might as well just use Erlang. We also looked at LFE and came to largely the same conclusion.

But, I applaud the effort and I plan to keep an eye on the project. We need more of these kinds of developments on BEAM, and hopefully some of their good ideas will trickle into the Erlang language itself.
storyTitle: Elixir: Ruby-like Syntax and Homoiconicity for Erlang VM
outcome: Elixir powers Discord, Pinterest and Nubank and remains in active development.
outcomeDetail: José Valim released Elixir in 2012 as a Ruby-flavored language on the Erlang VM. Discord used it to handle five million concurrent users, Pinterest and Nubank adopted it, and Elixir kept shipping major releases through v1.20 in 2026.
note: metajack was right that Elixir keeps Erlang's semantics, but wrong that this made it pointless. Familiar syntax, macros and better tooling brought a new community to the BEAM.

author: skrebbel
cardQuote: Is Phoenix's routing somehow more powerful than that, for reasons that I'm missing, or is it just a Rails-ism blatantly ported over to Elixir?
quote:
Nice writeup. I hadn't looked at Phoenix yet.

It seems that many Elixir people come from Ruby. One thing we should be wary of is making shallow ports of Ruby concepts into Elixir, when there's much more elegant approaches available. We, software engineers, have a tendency of doing this: for example, there's a whole bucketload of C# libraries that have Java roots (NHibernate, Spring.NET), and every single one of them is a bloated piece of nonsense that doesn't make good use of C#'s strengths. We should avoid making Elixir a Ruby-on-Erlang when it has the potential to be so much more.

I haven't figured out yet to what extent Phoenix does this, but this blog post highlights some things that make me wonder.

For instance, the router confuses me. Is there any point in making an explicit router over just splitting the URL by "/" into a list and then just pattern matching on that?

e.g.

```
    def get(["users", user], _params) do
        # show stuff
    end

    def post(["users"], _params) do
        # store stuff
    end

    def get([], _params) do
        # show root page
    end

```

Is Phoenix's routing somehow more powerful than that, for reasons that I'm missing, or is it just a Rails-ism blatantly ported over to Elixir?
storyTitle: Programming in Elixir with the Phoenix Framework
outcome: Phoenix became Elixir's default web framework and spawned LiveView; Phoenix 1.7 shipped in 2023.
outcomeDetail: Chris McCord's framework reached 1.0 in 2015 and borrowed Rails conventions without staying a clone. Phoenix Channels and LiveView gave it a distinct real-time story, and Phoenix remains the standard way to build Elixir web apps.
note: skrebbel's worry about shallow Ruby ports was reasonable, and Phoenix did keep Rails-style routing. But channels, LiveView and Ecto helped it outgrow the 'Rails-ism' label.

author: nestlequ1k
cardQuote: This is how PHP dies. You end up with 100 frameworks, and it's impossible to hire anyone who has experience with the framework you are using.
quote: This is how PHP dies. You end up with 100 frameworks, and it's impossible to hire anyone who has experience with the framework you are using.
outcome: Laravel became PHP's most popular framework; Laravel 11 shipped in 2024.
outcomeDetail: Taylor Otwell's framework grew from a 2012 side project into the dominant PHP web framework. Laravel 11 arrived in 2024, Laravel Cloud launched in 2025, and PHP still runs most of the web.
note: nestlequ1k predicted that framework proliferation would kill PHP hiring. Instead Laravel consolidated much of the PHP market and made its own conventions a hiring standard.

author: mlevental
cardQuote: i don't understand why people do this - build these frameworks. it's hundreds of independent labor hours and forgoes the key value prop of python (or whatever language they're reimplementing the wheel in): the existing ecosystem.
quote:
honest,sincere question:

i don't understand why people do this - build these frameworks. it's hundreds of independent labor hours and forgoes the key value prop of python (or whatever language they're reimplementing the wheel in): the existing ecosystem. i would never use this over flask or django because the community around each of those frameworks. that includes plugins, docs, blog posts, SO posts, etc. further more i'm not going to trust that one shop will exist forever and maintain this framework to the same extent that django is maintained. so in effect by adopting this framework i take on the maintenance responsibility. but why would i ever do that? it's not interesting work (very little groundbreaking research left in the http server space i think), it's thankless, and it's just completely unnecessary - every time i submit a PR i'll be looking enviously at django foundation's latest release.

so why would anyone write something like this and why would anyone ever adopt? if you're going for speed without ecosystem then just use Go or Java or C# to begin with. is it just NIH syndrome?
storyTitle: Show HN: FastAPI: build Python APIs with Go-like speed and automatic UI docs
outcome: FastAPI became one of Python's most popular API frameworks; version 0.100 shipped in 2023.
outcomeDetail: Sebastián Ramírez released FastAPI in 2018; it combined Starlette, Pydantic and type hints into a framework with automatic OpenAPI docs. It became a default choice for new Python APIs and built a large community of its own.
note: mlevental was right that ecosystems matter, but wrong that FastAPI had no reason to exist. Type-driven validation and generated docs were a real gap.

author: the_duke
cardQuote: I don't see the point of yet another framework here.
quote:
Vue.js has single file components [1] and template precompilation [2] (or optionally JSX support, which is basically a precompiled template).

I don't see the point of yet another framework here.

The "no dependencies" argument seems to fall down for me, since it would seem to me that they would need to duplicate a lot of code for state management and rendering, bloating the code for anything more complex.

And if there's some clever tree shaking or whatever going on, than I don't see the point as opposed to just including another JS file...

I couldn't find any explanation of what's so different here, worthy of creating another framework for it. Would love to be enlightened!

[1] https://vuejs.org/v2/guide/single-file-components.html

[2] https://www.npmjs.com/package/vue-template-compiler
storyTitle: Svelte – A UI framework that compiles into tiny standalone JavaScript modules
outcome: SvelteKit 1.0 shipped in 2022; Svelte was Stack Overflow's most-loved web framework that year.
outcomeDetail: Rich Harris's compiler-first framework grew from a 2016 curiosity into one of the major frontend options. Svelte 3 rethought reactivity in 2019, SvelteKit 1.0 shipped in 2022, and Svelte 5 arrived in 2024.
note: the_duke saw Svelte as redundant next to Vue, but missed that compile-time reactivity and zero-runtime output were a distinct trade-off. Svelte's community grew around exactly that difference.

author: cphoover
cardQuote: I think this de-facto fork of node.js will only serve to create fragmentation, and confuse product owners about which platform to use.
quote: I think Deno is a mistake at this point... Yes we thank Ryan Dahl for his huge contributions to integrating libuv and v8 outside of a browser to create node.js but a lot of work has been created by a huge ecosystem of developers after this. I think this de-facto fork of node.js will only serve to create fragmentation, and confuse product owners about which platform to use.
outcome: Deno 2.0 shipped in 2024; Cloudflare hired the Deno team in 2026.
outcomeDetail: Ryan Dahl's runtime reached 1.0 in 2020 and 2.0 in 2024, adding npm compatibility and a package registry. In October 2026 Cloudflare announced it was hiring the entire Deno team and would support the runtime for one more year.
note: Deno did not become a de-facto Node fork or split the ecosystem; it stayed an alternative and found an acquirer. The 2026 wind-down means cphoover's 'mistake' call was not wholly wrong, just premature.

author: zitterbewegung
cardQuote: I wish you could use javascript because I really don't want to learn dart. I also don't really trust Google supporting yet another framework very long either.
quote: So they ported dart to be used on mobile with a mobile app toolkit? It looks like the system is similar to react native but it uses dart instead of javascript and also compiles to native code. I wish you could use javascript because I really don't want to learn dart. I also don't really trust Google supporting yet another framework very long either. I wish they had a sample mobile app instead of just a video on the main page.
storyTitle: Announcing Flutter beta 1: Build beautiful native apps
outcome: Flutter 1.0 shipped in 2018; Google says more than a million Flutter apps have been published.
outcomeDetail: Google's cross-platform toolkit moved from a 2015 experiment to a 2017 beta and 1.0 in December 2018. It is used by Google Pay, Alibaba and ByteDance, and Google has reported over a million Flutter apps on the stores.
note: zitterbewegung's distrust of Google's staying power was common, but Flutter outlasted many of its skeptics. The Dart aversion was real, yet Flutter's tooling won over mobile teams.

author: angersock
cardQuote: But instead, now there's yet another language without great innovation that is probably going to be badly supported outside of the Apple ecosystem but still will have enough fandom to keep it alive and make life annoying.
quote:
I'm not really that impressed--it looks like a hodgepodge of ideas from ES6, Ruby, Go, and maybe Rust, with a bit of backend work done to let it work on their existing infrastructure.

I dislike that Apple has continued the special snowflake approach, that for some reason we as developers need to learn yet another different-but-almost-the-same language to develop for them, instead of just adding proper support and documentation for an existing language. Why not just let us use ES6, or normal C/C++, or Java?

But instead, now there's yet another language without great innovation that is probably going to be badly supported outside of the Apple ecosystem but still will have enough fandom to keep it alive and make life annoying.

At least Google had the decency to pick a language everybody was already using and use that.

EDIT:

I feel bad for all the engineers stuck in those pixel mines, not allowed to talk about what they're doing, doomed to reinvent things that are on the way out just as they come in.
outcome: Swift was open-sourced in 2015 and became the default language for iOS and macOS; Swift 6 shipped in 2024.
outcomeDetail: Apple announced Swift at WWDC 2014 and open-sourced it the next year. It became the default language for iOS and macOS, expanded to server-side work through Vapor, and reached Swift 6 in 2024.
note: angersock was right that Swift remains Apple-centric, but wrong that it would be badly supported or uninventive. It replaced Objective-C far faster than most observers expected.

author: bufferoverflow
cardQuote: It reminds me more of jQuery. And while I see how it's great for quick prototyping, it's going to be a nightmare in a large project.
quote: It reminds me more of jQuery. And while I see how it's great for quick prototyping, it's going to be a nightmare in a large project. I really like React, where data and HTML are clearly separate. I don't want to send raw HTML back and forth, I want to send only data.
storyTitle: Htmx – high power tools for HTML
outcome: htmx joined GitHub Accelerator in 2023 and shipped htmx 2.0 in 2024.
outcomeDetail: Carson Gross's hypermedia library grew out of Intercooler.js and found a large audience tired of SPA complexity. htmx 2.0 landed in 2024, and the project became a standard option for server-rendered interactivity.
note: bufferoverflow was right that htmx is not a fit for every large app, but wrong that it would be a nightmare. Its HTML-over-the-wire model proved durable, especially alongside Django, Rails and Go.

author: Annatar
cardQuote: How is inventing yet another complicated machinery to churn out some HTML and JavaScript innovation?
quote: How is inventing yet another complicated machinery to churn out some HTML and JavaScript innovation?
storyTitle: Astro 1.0 – a web framework for building fast, content-focused websites
outcome: Astro is downloaded about a million times a week and joined Cloudflare in 2026.
outcomeDetail: Astro 1.0 shipped in August 2022 with an islands architecture for content-heavy sites. By 2026 it was seeing roughly a million weekly downloads and being used by Webflow, Wix, Microsoft and Google; Cloudflare acquired the Astro Technology Company in January 2026.
note: Annatar dismissed Astro as needless machinery, but the framework's static-first islands model found a real niche between static site generators and full SPAs.

author: unclebucknasty
cardQuote: I don't know why we need another framework that smashes together code and HTML/directive-based templates like this and, generally, keeps us bound so tightly to web idioms.
quote:
They lost me at: ``` return (
{projects.map((project) => ( {project.title} ))}
. . .
``` I don't know why we need another framework that smashes together code and HTML/directive-based templates like this and, generally, keeps us bound so tightly to web idioms. Would be nice to have a framework that obscures these kinds of "web fundamentals", so we no longer have to wrangle such low-level primitives to build complex apps. EDIT: The people downvoting this are suffering from a failure of imagination. Sure, Remix may be an improvement over some current frameworks' failings, but there's no reason improvements need to be so incremental or debt-bound.
storyTitle: Remix – A framework focused on web fundamentals and modern UX
outcome: Shopify acquired Remix in 2022; Remix merged with React Router in 2024.
outcomeDetail: Remix open-sourced in November 2021 and was acquired by Shopify less than a year later. Its loader and action model influenced React Router v7, which absorbed Remix in 2024.
note: unclebucknasty disliked the JSX/HTML mixing, but that was the React idiom Remix was built on. The framework's data-loading model proved influential enough to be folded into React Router.

author: lemevi
cardQuote: The days of separate templates are hopefully forever behind me. Not trying to dismiss your very hard work I'm sure, but React has taken us into the future.
quote:
> More importantly, there’s no need to worry about calling $apply in a timeout, or calling setState(), or listening to store events

Calling `setState` is not a big deal and neither is dealing with stores. It's very simple and you keep your state separate from your HTML.

At this point I probably can't do web development without JSX and not be miserable. The days of separate templates are hopefully forever behind me. Not trying to dismiss your very hard work I'm sure, but React has taken us into the future. Maybe with esperanto you could add templates into your own JS or make it work with JSX and react-dom.
outcome: Vue 3 shipped in 2020; Vue is used by GitLab and the Wikimedia Foundation.
outcomeDetail: Evan You's Vue reached 1.0 in October 2015 and grew into one of the big three frontend frameworks. Vue 3 arrived in 2020, and GitLab and Wikimedia both build major interfaces with it.
note: lemevi treated JSX and React as the endpoint of frontend history. Vue kept the template model alive and became the default in several large organizations.

author: thebluesky
cardQuote: Was expecting a Scala competitor, but found a slightly better Java with some syntax sugar.
quote:
Looks like a mildly cleaned up Java, was expecting something a little more interesting. Don't see much in the way of functional programming or worthwhile changes vs Java.

Was expecting a Scala competitor, but found a slightly better Java with some syntax sugar. It's "nice", but not really different enough to warrant the effort of switching to another language. As a Java dev for 10+ years Scala was an eye opener on what a language could really be, Kotlin is "nice", but sadly not that interesting.

Minor pet peave is they have retained even Java's verbosity for outputting text:

Kotlin:
System.out?.println("Hi")
Java:
System.out.println("Hi")
Scala:
println("Hi")
Ruby:
puts("Hi")
storyTitle: Web-based editor for Kotlin, JetBrains' new JVM language
outcome: Google made Kotlin a first-class Android language in 2017 and its preferred language in 2019.
outcomeDetail: JetBrains unveiled Kotlin in 2011 and shipped 1.0 in 2016. Google announced first-class Android support at I/O 2017 and made Kotlin its preferred Android language in 2019; it is also used for server-side JVM work.
note: thebluesky judged Kotlin as 'slightly better Java' and not worth switching for. Null safety, JetBrains tooling and Google's Android endorsement made it one of the most consequential JVM languages.

author: Meai
cardQuote: No IDE support, no VM in Chrome yet, also no support for calling existing javascript libraries. These three things guarantee no quick adoption. I have no idea what Google is thinking.
quote: No IDE support, no VM in Chrome yet, also no support for calling existing javascript libraries. These three things guarantee no quick adoption. I have no idea what Google is thinking.
storyTitle: Google introduces Dart, a new programming language for web applications
outcome: Dart's browser VM was dropped, but Flutter made Dart the language of more than a million apps.
outcomeDetail: Google unveiled Dart in 2011 as a JavaScript challenger. Chrome never shipped the Dart VM, but Dart 2 and Flutter gave the language a second life on mobile; Flutter passed a million published apps.
note: Meai was right that browser Dart would not be adopted quickly—Chrome dropped the VM in 2015. He was wrong that Google had no plan: Flutter turned Dart into a mobile success.
